concept.title: Self-Improving Proofs: Proofs That Get Simpler Over Time
concept.concept_description: Proofs are static objects, but what if proofs could improve? Define a proof refinement system where each proof P has a complexity C(P) = length(P) + depth(P) + number of lemmas, and a proof P' is a refinement of P if P' proves the same theorem with C(P') < C(P). Conjecture: For every theorem T provable in ZFC, there exists a sequence of refinements P = P_0, P_1, P_2, ... such that C(P_n) is non-increasing and the limit P_infinity is the simplest proof of T (in the sense of Kolmogorov complexity). Moreover, the refinement process halts: there exists N such that C(P_N) = C(P_{N+1}) = ... = C(P_infinity). The key insight: proof simplification is a well-founded process because the complexity is a natural number that decreases at each step. But the process can be arbitrarily long — the proof of the four-color theorem might require 10^100 refinements to reach its simplest form. Test: formalize the refinement system in Lean 4. Starting from the statement of the irrationality of sqrt(2), generate refinements by eliminating unnecessary lemmas, shortening case splits, and removing redundant quantifiers. Measure C(P) at each step and verify it decreases. Impact: proofs are not static — they are living objects that can be improved. The simplest proof of a theorem is the LIMIT of the refinement process, and this limit ALWAYS exists.

concept.lean_guess: Define proof complexity C(P) = length(P) + depth(P) + number_of_lemmas(P) for a proof P in a formal system. Define refinement: P' refines P if P' proves the same theorem as P and C(P') < C(P). Prove: the refinement process is well-founded — there is no infinite decreasing chain C(P_0) > C(P_1) > ... because C takes values in the natural numbers. Prove: the limit P_infinity exists because the chain must terminate at a proof of minimal complexity. Example: the proof of 'there exist n consecutive composite numbers' requires induction up to n, but the simplest proof uses only the factorial n! + 2, n! + 3, ..., n! + n. concept.title: Strong Δ-matroids are exactly those without peerless antipodes
concept.concept_description: Conjecture: A Δ-matroid M on a finite ground set E is strong (i.e., satisfies the symmetric basis exchange axiom) if and only if its system of feasible sets contains no peerless antipode. A peerless antipode is defined as an element e∈E for which there exist feasible sets A,B∈F(M) such that A△B={e} and for every feasible set C∈F(M) with e∈C we have C∖{e}∉F(M). This conjecture links the combinatorial notion of strength with the novel 'peerless' antipode characterisation introduced in the paper and is expected to be formalizable in Lean 4 using the existing Δ-matroid library.

concept.title: Godel's Casino: Incomplete but Winnable Games
concept.concept_description: Godel's incompleteness theorem says there are true statements that cannot be proved. But what if we turn incompleteness into a GAME? Define Godel's Casino: a game where the player bets on the truth value of statements that are independent of ZFC. The house deals cards representing arithmetic statements, and the player must bet TRUE or FALSE. The Continuum Hypothesis is the first card — you can bet either way and you're RIGHT in some model. Conjecture: Godel's Casino has a winning strategy that guarantees expected profit > 0, even though individual bets are undecidable. The strategy: bet TRUE on Sigma_1 statements (they're true if provable, and ZFC is Sigma_1-complete), bet FALSE on Pi_1 statements that are known to be independent (like Con(ZFC)), and bet on the CONSERVATIVE extension for statements that are genuinely undecidable. The expected profit per round is at least 1/3 because at least 1/3 of arithmetic statements are decidable (by the arithmetic hierarchy: the fraction of statements at level n that are decidable at level n is at least 1/3). Test: simulate Godel's Casino with 1000 independent ZFC statements and verify the winning strategy achieves expected profit > 0. Impact: incompleteness is not a barrier — it's an opportunity. You can WIN at the game of undecidability.

# Surreal Topology: A Bridge Between Combinatorial Game Theory and Point-Set Topology

Conway's surreal numbers `Surreal` form the largest totally ordered field, built out of
combinatorial games (`PGame`).  A natural topology to put on them is the **order topology**
(a.k.a. the *interval topology*), generated by the open rays `Set.Iio a` and `Set.Ioi a`,
equivalently by the open intervals `(a, b)`.

This file proves a cross-domain **connector theorem**:

> The order/interval topology on the surreal numbers is **disconnected**.

The bridge is between:

* *Combinatorial game theory / order theory*: the surreals are **non-Archimedean** — there is a
  single surreal number larger than every natural number.  This is a genuinely game-theoretic
  fact here, obtained from `Surreal.bddAbove_range_of_small`: any *set-sized* family of surreals
  is bounded above, and `ℕ` is set-sized, so `{0, 1, 2, …}` has a surreal upper bound.

* *Point-set topology*: that single non-Archimedean gap splits the line into two nonempty pieces
  that are simultaneously open and closed (a nontrivial *clopen* set), so the space cannot be
  (pre)connected.

The clopen set exhibited is the collection of **finite surreals**
`{x | ∃ n : ℕ, x < n}` — everything dominated by some natural number.  Its complement is the class
of infinitely large surreals.  Both are open in the order topology, so the finite surreals form a
nontrivial clopen set.

## Consequences (refuting the naive "connected / contractible" conjecture)

Because a path-connected (in particular, contractible) space is connected, the disconnectedness
result immediately shows the interval topology on `Surreal` is **not** connected, **not**
path-connected, and hence **not** contractible.  So the conjecture that the interval topology makes
`No` a connected, contractible space is *false*; the honest statement is the opposite.

* `Surreal.exists_gt_natCast` : non-Archimedean witness — a surreal above every natural number.
* `Surreal.finiteSurreals_isClopen` : the finite surreals form a clopen set.
* `Surreal.not_preconnectedSpace` : the interval topology on `Surreal` is disconnected.
* `Surreal.not_connectedSpace`, `Surreal.not_pathConnectedSpace` : corollaries.
* `Surreal.instT2Space` : as a positive counterpoint, the interval topology *is* Hausdorff.
-/

open Set

namespace Surreal

topology generated by the open rays, the `OrderTopology` instance holds by `rfl`.
-/

  Preorder.topology Surreal.{0}

instance instOrderTopology : OrderTopology Surreal.{0} := ⟨rfl⟩

order topology on a linear order. -/
instance instT2Space : T2Space Surreal.{0} := inferInstance

is bounded above.  Applying this to the natural numbers produces a surreal dominating every
natural number — a purely order/game-theoretic fact with no topological content.

number.  (The surreal upper bound of the set `{0, 1, 2, …}` exists because that set is small.) -/

  obtain ⟨M, hM⟩ := Surreal.bddAbove_range_of_small (fun n : ℕ => (n : Surreal.{0}))
  refine ⟨M + 1, fun n => ?_⟩
  have hle : (n : Surreal.{0}) ≤ M := hM ⟨n, rfl⟩
  have h1 : M < M + 1 := by linarith [zero_lt_one (α := Surreal.{0})]
  linarith

### The clopen set of finite surreals

/-- The **finite surreals**: those bounded above by some natural number. -/
def FiniteSurreals : Set Surreal.{0} := {x | ∃ n : ℕ, x < (n : Surreal.{0})}

/-- The finite surreals are open: they are the union of the open rays `Iio n`. -/
theorem finiteSurreals_isOpen : IsOpen FiniteSurreals := by
  have hrw : FiniteSurreals = ⋃ n : ℕ, Iio (n : Surreal.{0}) := by
    ext x; simp [FiniteSurreals]
  rw [hrw]
  exact isOpen_iUnion (fun _ => isOpen_Iio)

/-- The finite surreals are closed: their complement (the infinitely large surreals) is open,
since around any infinite surreal `x` the whole ray `Ioi (x - 1)` stays infinite. -/
theorem finiteSurreals_isClosed : IsClosed FiniteSurreals := by
  rw [← isOpen_compl_iff, isOpen_iff_forall_mem_open]
  intro x hx
  simp only [FiniteSurreals, mem_compl_iff, mem_setOf_eq, not_exists, not_lt] at hx
  refine ⟨Ioi (x - 1), ?_, isOpen_Ioi, by simp⟩
  intro y hy
  simp only [mem_Ioi] at hy
  simp only [FiniteSurreals, mem_compl_iff, mem_setOf_eq, not_exists, not_lt]
  intro n
  have hn : ((n : ℕ) : Surreal.{0}) + 1 ≤ x := by
    have := hx (n + 1)
    push_cast at this ⊢
    linarith
  linarith

  ⟨finiteSurreals_isClosed, finiteSurreals_isOpen⟩

  ⟨1, by norm_num⟩

/-- Some surreal is *not* finite (any non-Archimedean witness), so the clopen set is not
everything. -/

  obtain ⟨M, hM⟩ := exists_gt_natCast
  intro h
  have hMmem : M ∈ FiniteSurreals := by rw [h]; trivial
  obtain ⟨n, hn⟩ := hMmem
  exact absurd hn (not_lt.2 (le_of_lt (hM n)))

/-!
### The connector theorem and its topological corollaries
-/

/-- **Main connector theorem.**  The interval (order) topology on the surreal numbers is
disconnected: the finite surreals form a nontrivial clopen set.  This bridges the
game-theoretic non-Archimedean structure of `Surreal` with a point-set topological property,
and refutes the conjecture that the interval topology is connected. -/
theorem not_preconnectedSpace : ¬ PreconnectedSpace Surreal.{0} := by
  intro h
  rcases isClopen_iff.1 finiteSurreals_isClopen with h0 | h1
  · exact (h0 ▸ zero_mem_finiteSurreals : (0 : Surreal.{0}) ∈ (∅ : Set Surreal.{0}))
  · exact finiteSurreals_ne_univ h1

/-- The surreal line with the interval topology is not connected. -/
theorem not_connectedSpace : ¬ ConnectedSpace Surreal.{0} := by
  intro h
  exact not_preconnectedSpace h.toPreconnectedSpace

/-- The surreal line with the interval topology is not path-connected (hence not contractible):
a path-connected space is connected, but the surreals are disconnected. -/
theorem not_pathConnectedSpace : ¬ PathConnectedSpace Surreal.{0} := by
  intro h
  exact not_connectedSpace h.connectedSpace

end Surreal

  above and below (`a < a + 1`, `a - 1 < a`).

  topology on `Surreal` has *no isolated points*; i.e. `Surreal` is a perfect
  space (`𝓝[≠] x` is never trivial).  This is a topological statement deduced
  from a game-theoretic/order-theoretic fact.

  greatest surreal).

carries a natural topology that is dense-in-itself (perfect) and non-compact.

import Mathlib

open SetTheory PGame
open scoped Topology

namespace Surreal

/-- **Density of the surreals (order-theory / combinatorial-game bridge).**
Between any two surreal numbers `a < b` lies a third surreal.  The witness is
the numeric pre-game `{a | b}` with a single Left option `a` and a single Right
option `b`; it is numeric precisely because `a < b`, and by the basic
`moveLeft_lt` / `lt_moveRight` inequalities it sits strictly between `a` and `b`. -/
noncomputable instance instDenselyOrdered : DenselyOrdered Surreal := by
  constructor
  rintro a b hab
  induction a using Quotient.inductionOn with | _ x =>
  induction b using Quotient.inductionOn with | _ y =>
  obtain ⟨X, ox⟩ := x
  obtain ⟨Y, oy⟩ := y
  have hXY : X < Y := hab
  -- the "simplest number between": the numeric pre-game `{X | Y}`.
  set g : PGame := PGame.mk PUnit PUnit (fun _ => X) (fun _ => Y) with hg
  have hgnum : g.Numeric := Numeric.mk (fun _ _ => hXY) (fun _ => ox) (fun _ => oy)
  refine ⟨Surreal.mk g hgnum, ?_, ?_⟩
  · simpa [g] using Surreal.mk_moveLeft_lt_mk hgnum PUnit.unit
  · simpa [g] using Surreal.mk_lt_mk_moveRight hgnum PUnit.unit

/-- The surreals have no greatest element: `a < a + 1`. -/
instance instNoMaxOrder : NoMaxOrder Surreal := ⟨fun a => ⟨a + 1, lt_add_one a⟩⟩

/-- The surreals have no least element: `a - 1 < a`. -/
instance instNoMinOrder : NoMinOrder Surreal := ⟨fun a => ⟨a - 1, sub_one_lt a⟩⟩

/-- The order topology on the surreal numbers. -/
noncomputable instance instTopologicalSpace : TopologicalSpace Surreal :=
  Preorder.topology Surreal

/-- The chosen topology is by definition the order topology. -/
instance instOrderTopology : OrderTopology Surreal := ⟨rfl⟩

/-- The order topology on the surreals is Hausdorff. -/
instance t2Space : T2Space Surreal := inferInstance

/-- **Main bridge theorem.**  The order topology on the surreal numbers is a
*perfect space*: it has no isolated points.  Equivalently, for every surreal `x`
the punctured neighbourhood filter `𝓝[≠] x` is nontrivial.  This is a purely
topological conclusion drawn from the order-density of `Surreal`
(`instDenselyOrdered`), itself a combinatorial-game fact. -/
instance perfectSpace : PerfectSpace Surreal := by
  rw [perfectSpace_iff_forall_not_isolated]
  intro x
  infer_instance

/-- Restatement of the bridge: no surreal number is isolated in the order
topology. -/
theorem not_isolated (x : Surreal) : (𝓝[≠] x).NeBot := inferInstance

/-- The order topology on the surreals is **not compact**: were it compact there
would be a greatest surreal number, contradicting `instNoMaxOrder`. -/
theorem not_compactSpace : ¬ CompactSpace Surreal := by
  intro h
  obtain ⟨m, -, hm⟩ :=
    (isCompact_univ (X := Surreal)).exists_isGreatest ⟨0, Set.mem_univ 0⟩
  obtain ⟨y, hy⟩ := exists_gt m
  exact absurd (hm (Set.mem_univ y)) (not_le.2 hy)

end Surreal

# Computational Evidence — Surreal Topology Bridge

The formal result is a *bridge* between combinatorial game theory / order theory
(Conway's surreal numbers) and point-set topology.  The central lemma is order
density; the topological consequences (perfect, Hausdorff, non-compact) then
follow from general Mathlib order-topology theory.  Below is the small-case
evidence for density, the fact everything hinges on.

## 1. The "simplest number between" construction

For surreals `a < b`, the witness placed strictly between them is the numeric
pre-game `{a | b}` (one Left option `a`, one Right option `b`).  This is exactly
Conway's *simplicity* construction.  Small cases:

| `a`   | `b`   | `{a | b}` (simplest surreal strictly between) |
|-------|-------|-----------------------------------------------|
| `0`   | `1`   | `1/2`                                          |
| `0`   | `2`   | `1`                                            |
| `-1`  | `1`   | `0`                                            |
| `1/2` | `1`   | `3/4`                                          |
| `0`   | `1/2` | `1/4`                                          |
| `0`   | `ω`   | `1` (finite ordinal, simplest positive)        |
| `0`   | `1/ω` | a positive infinitesimal (e.g. `1/(2ω)`)       |

The construction never fails: `{a | b}` is numeric iff every Left option is
`<` every Right option, i.e. iff `a < b`, which is exactly the hypothesis.  This
is what the Lean proof of `Surreal.instDenselyOrdered` formalizes: `a < b` gives
`Numeric {a | b}`, and `moveLeft_lt` / `lt_moveRight` give `a < {a|b} < b`.

## 2. Density holds even across "scales"

Density is not just a real-number phenomenon here — it holds between
infinitesimally close surreals too:

* between `1/ω` and `2/ω` sits `3/(2ω)`;
* between `0` and every positive infinitesimal sits a smaller positive
  infinitesimal (`ε ↦ {0 | ε}`);
* between `ω` and `ω + 1` sits `ω + 1/2`.

So there are no isolated points at any scale, which is precisely the input to
the topological conclusion (`PerfectSpace`).

## 3. Counterexample hunt (unboundedness / non-compactness)

We tested the universal claims that `Surreal` has no top and no bottom:

* `a < a + 1` for all `a` (used for `NoMaxOrder`);
* `a - 1 < a` for all `a` (used for `NoMinOrder`).

Both hold in every strict ordered ring with `0 < 1`, and `Surreal` is one
(`IsStrictOrderedRing Surreal` in Mathlib).  No counterexample exists; a
counterexample would require a greatest/least surreal, but `a + 1` / `a - 1`
always escape any candidate.  Non-compactness of the order topology is the
topological shadow of this.

## 4. Why no OEIS sequence

The result is structural (a topological classification statement), not an
enumeration, so no integer sequence is attached.  The relevant "counts" (e.g.
the number of surreals of a given birthday) are the well-known powers of two /
`2^ω` cardinalities and are not the object of this bridge.

All claims above are confirmed by the compiling Lean file
`SurrealTopologyBridge.lean` (checked to depend only on the standard axioms
`propext`, `Classical.choice`, `Quot.sound`).

# Future Directions — Surreal Topology

## What was proved

The surreal-topology deliverable establishes a cross-domain bridge between
Conway's surreal numbers (combinatorial game theory / set theory) and point-set
topology, using Mathlib's `Surreal` type (numeric pre-games modulo game
equivalence, a genuine `Type` in one Lean universe). All results below compile
end-to-end and depend only on the standard axioms `propext`, `Classical.choice`,
`Quot.sound`.

### `SurrealTopologyBridge.lean` — density and the perfect-space bridge

1. `Surreal.instDenselyOrdered` — the surreals are densely ordered; the witness
   between `a < b` is the simplest number `{a | b}` (a combinatorial-game
   construction).
2. `Surreal.instNoMaxOrder`, `Surreal.instNoMinOrder` — unbounded above/below.
3. `Surreal.t2Space` — the order topology is Hausdorff.
4. `Surreal.perfectSpace` / `Surreal.not_isolated` — **bridge theorem**: the
   order topology has no isolated points (it is a perfect space / dense in
   itself). A topological conclusion drawn from an order/game-theoretic fact.
5. `Surreal.not_compactSpace` — the order topology is not compact.

### `SurrealDisconnected.lean` — the interval topology is disconnected

The naive conjecture that the interval topology on `No` is connected /
contractible is **false**; the honest statement is the opposite, and it is now
proved:

1. `Surreal.exists_gt_natCast` — **non-Archimedean witness**: a surreal strictly
   larger than every natural number (the surreal upper bound of the *small* set
   `{0, 1, 2, …}`). Purely order/game-theoretic.
2. `Surreal.finiteSurreals_isClopen` — the finite surreals `{x | ∃ n, x < n}`
   form a nontrivial clopen set (open as a union of rays `Iio n`; closed because
   around any infinite surreal the whole ray `Ioi (x-1)` stays infinite).
3. `Surreal.not_preconnectedSpace` — **connector theorem**: the interval/order
   topology on `Surreal` is disconnected.
4. `Surreal.not_connectedSpace`, `Surreal.not_pathConnectedSpace` — corollaries;
   in particular the surreal line is **not** path-connected, hence **not**
   contractible.
5. `Surreal.instT2Space` — positive counterpoint: the interval topology is still
   Hausdorff.

### `SurrealTopologyDeep.lean` — order-gap ↔ topology theory

General structural theory of linearly ordered spaces underpinning the above:

* `OrderGap`, `GapFree` — Dedekind gaps and their absence.
* `gapFree_of_conditionallyComplete`, `gapFree_of_connectedSpace` — completeness
  and connectedness both forbid gaps.
* `OrderGap.lower_isOpen`, `OrderGap.upper_isOpen` — a gap yields a clopen split.
* `rat_not_connectedSpace`, `int_not_connectedSpace`, `real_connectedSpace` —
  the `ℚ`/`ℤ`/`ℝ` reference points for the gap–connectedness duality.
* Auxiliary: `orderIso_continuous`(`_inv`), `dense_order_separation`,
  `archimedean_bound`, `noncompactSpace_of_noMinOrder`,
  `hasCountableLocalBasis_of_secondCountable`, `real_has_countable_local_basis`.

## Relationship to the original conjecture (honest assessment)

The mission statement made several strong claims; the formalization corrects
them:

* **"The interval topology makes No connected."** *False* for the order topology
  inside a single universe: `Surreal` is non-Archimedean, and the finite
  surreals form a nontrivial clopen set, so the space is disconnected
  (`Surreal.not_preconnectedSpace`). Density alone never gives connectedness
  (`ℚ` is the standard counterexample, `rat_not_connectedSpace`).

* **"No has no gaps (every Dedekind cut is filled)."** True only cut-by-cut for
  *set*-sized cuts; as a class `No` has gaps, and the non-Archimedean cut
  (finite vs. infinite surreals) is exactly the clopen split that disconnects the
  space. Connectedness of a linear order in the order topology requires Dedekind
  completeness, which fails.

* **"No is contractible; π₁(No) = 0."** *False* for the order topology: a
  contractible space is path-connected and hence connected, contradicting
  `Surreal.not_connectedSpace`. The proposed homotopy `H(x,t) = x·{t|0}` cannot

The provable, correct core is: the order/interval topology on the surreals is
**dense-in-itself (perfect), Hausdorff, non-compact, and disconnected** — the
non-Archimedean gap is what does the disconnecting.

## Concrete next steps

1. **Total disconnectedness.** We exhibit one clopen split; strengthen to

   with a clopen set (e.g. via translated/scaled non-Archimedean gaps, or
   real/ordinal cuts).

2. **Topological ring structure.** Investigate whether `(Surreal, order
   topology)` is a `TopologicalAddGroup` / `TopologicalRing`. Continuity of
   addition holds for order topologies on ordered groups; multiplication is more
   delicate without an Archimedean property.

3. **The interval topology vs. the order topology.** Define the topology

   whether the coarser topology is still disconnected.

4. **Proper-class formalization.** A fully faithful treatment of `No` as a proper

   `Type`; the current results live in one universe `Surreal.{0}`.

5. **Real embedding.** Formalize the order embedding `ℝ ↪ Surreal` and transfer
   the standard topology, connecting classical analysis to surreal topology.

The differential sends a vertex function to the difference of its values at the edge endpoints. We prove that its Euler characteristic equals the combinatorial Euler characteristic |V|−|E|, that H⁰ consists exactly of the globally constant functions (the meme is perfectly consistent), and that for a connected graph dim H⁰ संग्रह = 1 while dim H¹ equals the first Betti number |E|−|V|+1. concept.mathematical_framing: A meme is a unit of cultural information that replicates through human minds. Define meme fitness as the sheaf cohomology group H^1(G, M) where G is the social network and M is the meme sheaf. import Mathlib

/-!
# A bridge: sheaf cohomology of graphs ↔ combinatorial graph invariants

This file connects two areas that at first glance are unrelated:

* **homological algebra / sheaf cohomology** — the cohomology groups `H⁰` and `H¹`
  of the *constant sheaf* on a graph, and
* **graph theory** — the Euler characteristic `|V| − |E|`, connectivity, and the
  first Betti number (cycle rank) `|E| − |V| + 1`.

## The model (the "meme sheaf")

A finite graph is given by a finite vertex type `V`, a finite edge type `E`, and
incidence maps `head tail : E → V`.  The **constant sheaf** with stalk a field `K`
gives the two-term cochain complex

```
0 → C⁰ = (V → K) --δ--> C¹ = (E → K) → 0 ,      (δ f)(e) = f (tail e) − f (head e).
```

We set `H⁰ = ker δ` (globally consistent sections — "interpretations" of the meme)
and `H¹ = C¹ / im δ` (obstructions to consistent transmission).

## Main results

* `cohomology_euler_characteristic` — abstract rank–nullity phrased cohomologically:
  for any linear map `δ` between finite-dimensional spaces,
  `dim (ker δ) − dim (coker δ) = dim C⁰ − dim C¹`.
* `graph_euler_characteristic` — the bridge:
  `dim H⁰ − dim H¹ = |V| − |E|`.
* `mem_ker_cobound_iff` — membership in `H⁰` is exactly consistency across edges.
* `H0_finrank_eq_one_of_connected` — for a connected (nonempty) graph, `dim H⁰ = 1`.
* `H1_finrank_of_connected` — hence the **first Betti number**:
  `dim H¹ = |E| − |V| + 1`.
-/

namespace SheafCohomologyGraphBridge

open Module

/-! ## Abstract cohomological Euler characteristic (homological algebra side) -/

/-- **Cohomological Euler characteristic.**  For a linear map `δ : C⁰ → C¹` between
finite-dimensional vector spaces, the alternating sum of the dimensions of its
kernel (`H⁰`) and cokernel (`H¹`) equals the alternating sum of the dimensions of
the cochain spaces.  This is rank–nullity, phrased as a statement about cohomology. -/
theorem cohomology_euler_characteristic
    {K C0 C1 : Type*} [Field K]
    [AddCommGroup C0] [Module K C0] [FiniteDimensional K C0]
    [AddCommGroup C1] [Module K C1] [FiniteDimensional K C1] (δ : C0 →ₗ[K] C1) :
    (finrank K (LinearMap.ker δ) : ℤ) - finrank K (C1 ⧸ LinearMap.range δ)
      = (finrank K C0 : ℤ) - finrank K C1 := by
  have h1 := LinearMap.finrank_range_add_finrank_ker δ
  have h2 := Submodule.finrank_quotient_add_finrank (LinearMap.range δ)
  omega

/-! ## The constant sheaf on a finite graph (graph-theory side) -/

variable {K : Type*} [Field K]
variable {V E : Type*} [Fintype V] [Fintype E] [DecidableEq V]

/-- The coboundary of the constant sheaf: `(δ f)(e) = f (tail e) − f (head e)`.
It measures how much a candidate "meaning" `f` fails to be consistent across each
communication edge. -/
def cobound (head tail : E → V) : (V → K) →ₗ[K] (E → K) where
  toFun f := fun e => f (tail e) - f (head e)
  map_add' f g := by funext e; simp; ring
  map_smul' c f := by funext e; simp; ring

/-- `H⁰(G, K)` — the zeroth cohomology (global consistent sections). -/
abbrev H0 (head tail : E → V) : Submodule K (V → K) := LinearMap.ker (cobound (K := K) head tail)

/-- `H¹(G, K)` — the first cohomology (cokernel of the coboundary). -/
abbrev H1 (head tail : E → V) := (E → K) ⧸ LinearMap.range (cobound (K := K) head tail)

omit [Fintype E] [DecidableEq V] in
/-- The dimension of `C⁰ = (V → K)` is the number of vertices. -/
theorem finrank_C0 : finrank K (V → K) = Fintype.card V := by
  simp [Module.finrank_fintype_fun_eq_card]

omit [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V] in
/-- The dimension of `C¹ = (E → K)` is the number of edges. -/
theorem finrank_C1 : finrank K (E → K) = Fintype.card E := by
  simp [Module.finrank_fintype_fun_eq_card]

omit [DecidableEq V] in
/-- **The bridge (Euler characteristic of a graph sheaf).**  The alternating sum of
the cohomology dimensions of the constant sheaf equals the graph's Euler
characteristic `|V| − |E|`. -/
theorem graph_euler_characteristic (head tail : E → V) :
    (finrank K (H0 (K := K) head tail) : ℤ) - finrank K (H1 (K := K) head tail)
      = (Fintype.card V : ℤ) - Fintype.card E := by
  have h := cohomology_euler_characteristic (cobound (K := K) head tail)
  rw [finrank_C0, finrank_C1] at h
  exact h

/-! ## Connectivity ↔ dimension of `H⁰` -/

/-- Reachability in the graph: the equivalence relation generated by the edges. -/
def Reach (head tail : E → V) : V → V → Prop :=
  Relation.EqvGen (fun a b => ∃ e, head e = a ∧ tail e = b)

/-- A graph is connected when every pair of vertices is reachable. -/
def GraphConnected (head tail : E → V) : Prop := ∀ u v : V, Reach head tail u v

omit [Fintype V] [Fintype E] [DecidableEq V] in
/-- Membership in `H⁰` means exactly consistency across every edge. -/
theorem mem_ker_cobound_iff (head tail : E → V) (f : V → K) :
    f ∈ H0 (K := K) head tail ↔ ∀ e, f (head e) = f (tail e) := by
  simp only [H0, LinearMap.mem_ker, cobound, LinearMap.coe_mk, AddHom.coe_mk, funext_iff,
    Pi.zero_apply, sub_eq_zero]
  exact forall_congr' (fun e => eq_comm)

omit [Field K] [Fintype V] [Fintype E] [DecidableEq V] in
/-- A consistent section is constant along reachability. -/
theorem eq_of_reach (head tail : E → V) (f : V → K)
    (hf : ∀ e, f (head e) = f (tail e)) {u v : V} (h : Reach head tail u v) :
    f u = f v := by
  induction h with
  | rel x y hxy => obtain ⟨e, rfl, rfl⟩ := hxy; exact hf e
  | refl x => rfl
  | symm x y _ ih => exact ih.symm
  | trans x y z _ _ ih1 ih2 => exact ih1.trans ih2

omit [Fintype V] [Fintype E] [DecidableEq V] in
/-- On a connected graph, every consistent section is a constant function. -/
theorem const_of_connected (head tail : E → V) (hconn : GraphConnected head tail)
    (f : V → K) (hf : f ∈ H0 (K := K) head tail) (u v : V) : f u = f v := by
  rw [mem_ker_cobound_iff] at hf
  exact eq_of_reach head tail f hf (hconn u v)

omit [Fintype E] [DecidableEq V] in
/-- **Connectivity ↔ `H⁰` is one-dimensional.**  For a connected nonempty graph, the
only globally consistent sections are the constant functions, so `dim H⁰ = 1`. -/
theorem H0_finrank_eq_one_of_connected [Nonempty V] (head tail : E → V)
    (hconn : GraphConnected head tail) :
    finrank K (H0 (K := K) head tail) = 1 := by
  refine finrank_eq_one_iff'.mpr ?_
  refine ⟨⟨fun _ => 1, ?_⟩, ?_, ?_⟩
  all_goals norm_num [Subtype.ext_iff]
  · ext; simp +decide [cobound]
  · exact fun h => by simpa using congr_fun h (Classical.arbitrary V)
  · intro f hf
    use f (Classical.arbitrary V)
    ext v
    simp_all +decide [funext_iff, cobound]
    exact eq_of_reach head tail f (fun e => sub_eq_zero.mp (hf e) ▸ rfl) (hconn _ _) ▸ rfl

omit [DecidableEq V] in
/-- **First Betti number (cycle rank) via cohomology.**  For a connected nonempty
graph, `dim H¹ = |E| − |V| + 1`.  This is the graph-theoretic circuit rank,
recovered as the dimension of the first sheaf cohomology. -/
theorem H1_finrank_of_connected [Nonempty V] (head tail : E → V)
    (hconn : GraphConnected head tail) :
    (finrank K (H1 (K := K) head tail) : ℤ)
      = (Fintype.card E : ℤ) - Fintype.card V + 1 := by
  have hEuler := graph_euler_characteristic (K := K) head tail
  have hH0 := H0_finrank_eq_one_of_connected (K := K) head tail hconn
  rw [hH0] at hEuler
  omega

/-! ## A concrete instance: the star tree (a "universally transmissible meme")

The star graph on `n+1` vertices has a center vertex `0` joined to each of the `n`
leaves.  It is a tree, so the meme sheaf has *no* consistency obstruction: `H¹ = 0`.
This is the extreme case of the bridge where the cycle rank vanishes. -/

/-- Incidence (`head`) of the star graph on `n+1` vertices: every edge starts at the
center vertex `0`. -/
def starHead (n : ℕ) : Fin n → Fin (n + 1) := fun _ => 0

/-- Incidence (`tail`) of the star graph on `n+1` vertices: edge `i` ends at leaf
`i.succ`. -/
def starTail (n : ℕ) : Fin n → Fin (n + 1) := fun i => i.succ

/-- The star graph is connected: every vertex is reachable from the center `0`. -/
theorem star_connected (n : ℕ) : GraphConnected (starHead n) (starTail n) := by
  -- Every vertex is reachable from the center `0`; connectedness then follows
  -- because `Reach` is an equivalence relation.
  have h_path : ∀ u : Fin (n + 1), Reach (starHead n) (starTail n) u 0 := by
    intro u
    induction u using Fin.induction with
    | zero => exact Relation.EqvGen.refl _
    | succ i _ => exact Relation.EqvGen.symm _ _ (Relation.EqvGen.rel _ _ ⟨i, rfl, rfl⟩)
  intro u v
  exact Relation.EqvGen.trans _ _ _ (h_path u) (Relation.EqvGen.symm _ _ (h_path v))

/-- **The star tree has vanishing `H¹`.**  As a tree it is a "universally
transmissible meme": there is no obstruction to consistent transmission. -/
theorem star_H1_finrank_zero {K : Type*} [Field K] (n : ℕ) :
    finrank K (H1 (K := K) (starHead n) (starTail n)) = 0 := by
  have h := H1_finrank_of_connected (K := K) (starHead n) (starTail n) (star_connected n)
  simp only [Fintype.card_fin] at h
  have : (finrank K (H1 (K := K) (starHead n) (starTail n)) : ℤ) = 0 := by push_cast at h ⊢; omega
  exact_mod_cast this

end SheafCohomologyGraphBridge

/-
# Surreal Topology: A Bridge Between Combinatorial Game Theory and Point-Set Topology

Conway's surreal numbers `Surreal` form the largest totally ordered field, built out of
combinatorial games (`PGame`).  A natural topology to put on them is the **order topology**
(a.k.a. the *interval topology*), generated by the open rays `Set.Iio a` and `Set.Ioi a`,
equivalently by the open intervals `(a, b)`.

This file proves a cross-domain **connector theorem**:

> The order/interval topology on the surreal numbers is **disconnected**.

The bridge is between:

* *Combinatorial game theory / order theory*: the surreals are **non-Archimedean** — there is a
  single surreal number larger than every natural number.  This is a genuinely game-theoretic
  fact here, obtained from `Surreal.bddAbove_range_of_small`: any *set-sized* family of surreals
  is bounded above, and `ℕ` is set-sized, so `{0, 1, 2, …}` has a surreal upper bound.

* *Point-set topology*: that single non-Archimedean gap splits the line into two nonempty pieces
  that are simultaneously open and closed (a nontrivial *clopen* set), so the space cannot be
  (pre)connected.

The clopen set exhibited is the collection of **finite surreals**
`{x | ∃ n : ℕ, x < n}` — everything dominated by some natural number.  Its complement is the class
of infinitely large surreals.  Both are open in the order topology, so the finite surreals form a
nontrivial clopen set.

## Consequences (refuting the naive "connected / contractible" conjecture)

Because a path-connected (in particular, contractible) space is connected, the disconnectedness
result immediately shows the interval topology on `Surreal` is **not** connected, **not**
path-connected, and hence **not** contractible.  So the conjecture that the interval topology makes
`No` a connected, contractible space is *false*; the honest statement is the opposite.

## Main results

* `Surreal.exists_gt_natCast` : non-Archimedean witness — a surreal above every natural number.
* `Surreal.finiteSurreals_isClopen` : the finite surreals form a clopen set.
* `Surreal.not_preconnectedSpace` : the interval topology on `Surreal` is disconnected.
* `Surreal.not_connectedSpace`, `Surreal.not_pathConnectedSpace` : corollaries.
* `Surreal.instT2Space` : as a positive counterpoint, the interval topology *is* Hausdorff.
-/

import Mathlib

open Set

namespace Surreal

/-!
### The interval (order) topology on the surreal numbers

We equip `Surreal.{0}` with the order topology.  Since `Preorder.topology` is *defined* as the
topology generated by the open rays, the `OrderTopology` instance holds by `rfl`.
-/

noncomputable instance instTopologicalSpace : TopologicalSpace Surreal.{0} :=
  Preorder.topology Surreal.{0}

instance instOrderTopology : OrderTopology Surreal.{0} := ⟨rfl⟩

/-- Positive counterpoint: the interval topology on the surreals is Hausdorff, being the
order topology on a linear order. -/
instance instT2Space : T2Space Surreal.{0} := inferInstance

/-!
### The game-theoretic ingredient: the surreals are non-Archimedean

`Surreal.bddAbove_range_of_small` says any family of surreals indexed by a *set* (a `Small` type)
is bounded above.  Applying this to the natural numbers produces a surreal dominating every
natural number — a purely order/game-theoretic fact with no topological content.
-/

/-- **Non-Archimedean witness.**  There is a surreal number strictly greater than every natural
number.  (The surreal upper bound of the set `{0, 1, 2, …}` exists because that set is small.) -/
theorem exists_gt_natCast : ∃ M : Surreal.{0}, ∀ n : ℕ, (n : Surreal.{0}) < M := by
  obtain ⟨M, hM⟩ := Surreal.bddAbove_range_of_small (fun n : ℕ => (n : Surreal.{0}))
  refine ⟨M + 1, fun n => ?_⟩
  have hle : (n : Surreal.{0}) ≤ M := hM ⟨n, rfl⟩
  have h1 : M < M + 1 := by linarith [zero_lt_one (α := Surreal.{0})]
  linarith

/-!
### The clopen set of finite surreals
-/

/-- The **finite surreals**: those bounded above by some natural number. -/
def FiniteSurreals : Set Surreal.{0} := {x | ∃ n : ℕ, x < (n : Surreal.{0})}

/-- The finite surreals are open: they are the union of the open rays `Iio n`. -/
theorem finiteSurreals_isOpen : IsOpen FiniteSurreals := by
  have hrw : FiniteSurreals = ⋃ n : ℕ, Iio (n : Surreal.{0}) := by
    ext x; simp [FiniteSurreals]
  rw [hrw]
  exact isOpen_iUnion (fun _ => isOpen_Iio)

/-- The finite surreals are closed: their complement (the infinitely large surreals) is open,
since around any infinite surreal `x` the whole ray `Ioi (x - 1)` stays infinite. -/
theorem finiteSurreals_isClosed : IsClosed FiniteSurreals := by
  rw [← isOpen_compl_iff, isOpen_iff_forall_mem_open]
  intro x hx
  simp only [FiniteSurreals, mem_compl_iff, mem_setOf_eq, not_exists, not_lt] at hx
  refine ⟨Ioi (x - 1), ?_, isOpen_Ioi, by simp⟩
  intro y hy
  simp only [mem_Ioi] at hy
  simp only [FiniteSurreals, mem_compl_iff, mem_setOf_eq, not_exists, not_lt]
  intro n
  have hn : ((n : ℕ) : Surreal.{0}) + 1 ≤ x := by
    have := hx (n + 1)
    push_cast at this ⊢
    linarith
  linarith

/-- The finite surreals form a nontrivial **clopen** set. -/
theorem finiteSurreals_isClopen : IsClopen FiniteSurreals :=
  ⟨finiteSurreals_isClosed, finiteSurreals_isOpen⟩

/-- `0` is a finite surreal, so the clopen set is nonempty. -/
theorem zero_mem_finiteSurreals : (0 : Surreal.{0}) ∈ FiniteSurreals :=
  ⟨1, by norm_num⟩

/-- Some surreal is *not* finite (any non-Archimedean witness), so the clopen set is not
everything. -/
theorem finiteSurreals_ne_univ : FiniteSurreals ≠ (univ : Set Surreal.{0}) := by
  obtain ⟨M, hM⟩ := exists_gt_natCast
  intro h
  have hMmem : M ∈ FiniteSurreals := by rw [h]; trivial
  obtain ⟨n, hn⟩ := hMmem
  exact absurd hn (not_lt.2 (le_of_lt (hM n)))

/-!
### The connector theorem and its topological corollaries
-/

/-- **Main connector theorem.**  The interval (order) topology on the surreal numbers is
disconnected: the finite surreals form a nontrivial clopen set.  This bridges the
game-theoretic non-Archimedean structure of `Surreal` with a point-set topological property,
and refutes the conjecture that the interval topology is connected. -/
theorem not_preconnectedSpace : ¬ PreconnectedSpace Surreal.{0} := by
  intro h
  rcases isClopen_iff.1 finiteSurreals_isClopen with h0 | h1
  · exact (h0 ▸ zero_mem_finiteSurreals : (0 : Surreal.{0}) ∈ (∅ : Set Surreal.{0}))
  · exact finiteSurreals_ne_univ h1

/-- The surreal line with the interval topology is not connected. -/
theorem not_connectedSpace : ¬ ConnectedSpace Surreal.{0} := by
  intro h
  exact not_preconnectedSpace h.toPreconnectedSpace

/-- The surreal line with the interval topology is not path-connected (hence not contractible):
a path-connected space is connected, but the surreals are disconnected. -/
theorem not_pathConnectedSpace : ¬ PathConnectedSpace Surreal.{0} := by
  intro h
  exact not_connectedSpace h.connectedSpace

end Surreal

# Computational Evidence: Sheaf Cohomology of Graphs ↔ Graph Invariants

## The bridge

We model a "meme" as the **constant sheaf** `K` on a finite graph `G = (V, E)` with
incidence maps `head, tail : E → V`. The cochain complex is

```
0 → C⁰ = (V → K) --δ--> C¹ = (E → K) → 0 ,      (δf)(e) = f(tail e) − f(head e).
```

Cohomology:
* `H⁰ = ker δ` — global consistent "interpretations" (sections of the meme sheaf).
* `H¹ = coker δ = C¹ / im δ` — obstructions to consistent transmission.

The **connector theorem** links a *homological* quantity (the alternating sum of
cohomology dimensions) to a purely *combinatorial* one (the vertex/edge count):

```
dim H⁰ − dim H¹ = |V| − |E|      (Euler characteristic).
```

For a **connected** graph, `dim H⁰ = 1`, so

```
dim H¹ = |E| − |V| + 1           (first Betti number / cycle rank).
```

This is the graph-theory ↔ homological-algebra bridge: the number of independent
cycles of a graph equals the dimension of the first sheaf cohomology of its
constant sheaf.

## Small-case calculations

| Graph            | \|V\| | \|E\| | connected | dim H⁰ | dim H¹ = \|E\|−\|V\|+1 |
|------------------|------|------|-----------|--------|------------------------|
| single vertex    | 1    | 0    | yes       | 1      | 0                      |
| edge (2 vtx)     | 2    | 1    | yes       | 1      | 0                      |
| path P₃          | 3    | 2    | yes       | 1      | 0                      |
| triangle C₃      | 3    | 3    | yes       | 1      | 1                      |
| cycle Cₙ         | n    | n    | yes       | 1      | 1                      |
| tree, n vertices | n    | n−1  | yes       | 1      | 0                      |
| K₄               | 4    | 6    | yes       | 1      | 3                      |
| two disjoint edges | 4  | 2    | no        | 2      | 0                      |

All rows satisfy the Euler identity `dim H⁰ − dim H¹ = |V| − |E|`, and every
connected row satisfies `dim H¹ = |E| − |V| + 1`.

### Interpretation in the meme model
* A tree (`H¹ = 0`) is "universally transmissible": no consistency barriers.
* A graph with cycles (`H¹ > 0`) has interpretation loops: `dim H¹` counts the
  independent cycles that a consistent meaning must be checked around.
* Disconnected communities (`dim H⁰ > 1`) allow the meme to mean different things
  in different components.

## OEIS

The Euler characteristic `|V| − |E|` and the cycle rank `|E| − |V| + 1` are the
standard topological invariants of a 1-complex; the cycle rank of a connected
graph is the "circuit rank" / "first Betti number" (cf. OEIS descriptions of
circuit rank). No new integer sequence is introduced — the content is the
identity linking the two sides.

## Counterexample hunt

The Euler-characteristic identity is an instance of rank–nullity and holds for
*every* finite graph and *every* field, so no counterexample exists (verified
symbolically in the Lean development, not just on the table above). The
connected-case Betti formula requires connectivity; the "two disjoint edges" row
shows it genuinely fails without it (`dim H¹ = 0 ≠ |E|−|V|+1 = −1`), which is why
connectivity is a hypothesis of that theorem.

# Surreal Topology: A Bridge Between Combinatorial Game Theory and Point-Set Topology

Conway's surreal numbers `Surreal` form the largest totally ordered field, built out of
combinatorial games (`PGame`).  A natural topology to put on them is the **order topology**
(a.k.a. the *interval topology*), generated by the open rays `Set.Iio a` and `Set.Ioi a`,
equivalently by the open intervals `(a, b)`.

This file proves a cross-domain **connector theorem**:

> The order/interval topology on the surreal numbers is **disconnected**.

The bridge is between:

* *Combinatorial game theory / order theory*: the surreals are **non-Archimedean** — there is a
  single surreal number larger than every natural number.  This is a genuinely game-theoretic
  fact here, obtained from `Surreal.bddAbove_range_of_small`: any *set-sized* family of surreals
  is bounded above, and `ℕ` is set-sized, so `{0, 1, 2, …}` has a surreal upper bound.

* *Point-set topology*: that single non-Archimedean gap splits the line into two nonempty pieces
  that are simultaneously open and closed (a nontrivial *clopen* set), so the space cannot be
  (pre)connected.

The clopen set exhibited is the collection of **finite surreals**
`{x | ∃ n : ℕ, x < n}` — everything dominated by some natural number.  Its complement is the class
of infinitely large surreals.  Both are open in the order topology, so the finite surreals form a
nontrivial clopen set.

## Consequences (refuting the naive "connected / contractible" conjecture)

Because a path-connected (in particular, contractible) space is connected, the disconnectedness
result immediately shows the interval topology on `Surreal` is **not** connected, **not**
path-connected, and hence **not** contractible.  So the conjecture that the interval topology makes
`No` a connected, contractible space is *false*; the honest statement is the opposite.

## Main results

* `Surreal.exists_gt_natCast` : non-Archimedean witness — a surreal above every natural number.
* `Surreal.finiteSurreals_isClopen` : the finite surreals form a clopen set.
* `Surreal.not_preconnectedSpace` : the interval topology on `Surreal` is disconnected.
* `Surreal.not_connectedSpace`, `Surreal.not_pathConnectedSpace` : corollaries.
* `Surreal.instT2Space` : as a positive counterpoint, the interval topology *is* Hausdorff.
-/

import Mathlib

open Set

namespace Surreal

/-!
### The interval (order) topology on the surreal numbers

We equip `Surreal.{0}` with the order topology.  Since `Preorder.topology` is *defined* as the
topology generated by the open rays, the `OrderTopology` instance holds by `rfl`.
-/

noncomputable instance instTopologicalSpace : TopologicalSpace Surreal.{0} :=
  Preorder.topology Surreal.{0}

instance instOrderTopology : OrderTopology Surreal.{0} := ⟨rfl⟩

/-- Positive counterpoint: the interval topology on the surreals is Hausdorff, being the
order topology on a linear order. -/
instance instT2Space : T2Space Surreal.{0} := inferInstance

/-!
### The game-theoretic ingredient: the surreals are non-Archimedean

`Surreal.bddAbove_range_of_small` says any family of surreals indexed by a *set* (a `Small` type)
is bounded above.  Applying this to the natural numbers produces a surreal dominating every
natural number — a purely order/game-theoretic fact with no topological content.
-/

/-- **Non-Archimedean witness.**  There is a surreal number strictly greater than every natural
number.  (The surreal upper bound of the set `{0, 1, 2, …}` exists because that set is small.) -/
theorem exists_gt_natCast : ∃ M : Surreal.{0}, ∀ n : ℕ, (n : Surreal.{0}) < M := by
  obtain ⟨M, hM⟩ := Surreal.bddAbove_range_of_small (fun n : ℕ => (n : Surreal.{0}))
  refine ⟨M + 1, fun n => ?_⟩
  have hle : (n : Surreal.{0}) ≤ M := hM ⟨n, rfl⟩
  have h1 : M < M + 1 := by linarith [zero_lt_one (α := Surreal.{0})]
  linarith

/-!
### The clopen set of finite surreals
-/

/-- The **finite surreals**: those bounded above by some natural number. -/
def FiniteSurreals : Set Surreal.{0} := {x | ∃ n : ℕ, x < (n : Surreal.{0})}

/-- The finite surreals are open: they are the union of the open rays `Iio n`. -/
theorem finiteSurreals_isOpen : IsOpen FiniteSurreals := by
  have hrw : FiniteSurreals = ⋃ n : ℕ, Iio (n : Surreal.{0}) := by
    ext x; simp [FiniteSurreals]
  rw [hrw]
  exact isOpen_iUnion (fun _ => isOpen_Iio)

/-- The finite surreals are closed: their complement (the infinitely large surreals) is open,
since around any infinite surreal `x` the whole ray `Ioi (x - 1)` stays infinite. -/
theorem finiteSurreals_isClosed : IsClosed FiniteSurreals := by
  rw [← isOpen_compl_iff, isOpen_iff_forall_mem_open]
  intro x hx
  simp only [FiniteSurreals, mem_compl_iff, mem_setOf_eq, not_exists, not_lt] at hx
  refine ⟨Ioi (x - 1), ?_, isOpen_Ioi, by simp⟩
  intro y hy
  simp only [mem_Ioi] at hy
  simp only [FiniteSurreals, mem_compl_iff, mem_setOf_eq, not_exists, not_lt]
  intro n
  have hn : ((n : ℕ) : Surreal.{0}) + 1 ≤ x := by
    have := hx (n + 1)
    push_cast at this ⊢
    linarith
  linarith

/-- The finite surreals form a nontrivial **clopen** set. -/
theorem finiteSurreals_isClopen : IsClopen FiniteSurreals :=
  ⟨finiteSurreals_isClosed, finiteSurreals_isOpen⟩

/-- `0` is a finite surreal, so the clopen set is nonempty. -/
theorem zero_mem_finiteSurreals : (0 : Surreal.{0}) ∈ FiniteSurreals :=
  ⟨1, by norm_num⟩

/-- Some surreal is *not* finite (any non-Archimedean witness), so the clopen set is not
everything. -/
theorem finiteSurreals_ne_univ : FiniteSurreals ≠ (univ : Set Surreal.{0}) := by
  obtain ⟨M, hM⟩ := exists_gt_natCast
  intro h
  have hMmem : M ∈ FiniteSurreals := by rw [h]; trivial
  obtain ⟨n, hn⟩ := hMmem
  exact absurd hn (not_lt.2 (le_of_lt (hM n)))

/-!
### The connector theorem and its topological corollaries
-/

/-- **Main connector theorem.**  The interval (order) topology on the surreal numbers is
disconnected: the finite surreals form a nontrivial clopen set.  This bridges the
game-theoretic non-Archimedean structure of `Surreal` with a point-set topological property,
and refutes the conjecture that the interval topology is connected. -/
theorem not_preconnectedSpace : ¬ PreconnectedSpace Surreal.{0} := by
  intro h
  rcases isClopen_iff.1 finiteSurreals_isClopen with h0 | h1
  · exact (h0 ▸ zero_mem_finiteSurreals : (0 : Surreal.{0}) ∈ (∅ : Set Surreal.{0}))
  · exact finiteSurreals_ne_univ h1

/-- The surreal line with the interval topology is not connected. -/
theorem not_connectedSpace : ¬ ConnectedSpace Surreal.{0} := by
  intro h
  exact not_preconnectedSpace h.toPreconnectedSpace

/-- The surreal line with the interval topology is not path-connected (hence not contractible):
a path-connected space is connected, but the surreals are disconnected. -/
theorem not_pathConnectedSpace : ¬ PathConnectedSpace Surreal.{0} := by
  intro h
  exact not_connectedSpace h.connectedSpace

end Surreal

# The L-Function Universe — A Cosmic Census, Part I: The Countable Side

This file formalizes the *positive* half of a census of L-functions, in the spirit of
the Selberg class programme.

## Background

An analytic L-function is (up to normalization) determined by its Dirichlet coefficients
`a : ℕ → ℂ`.  The *Selberg class* `S` is the set of such Dirichlet series subject to four
axioms: analytic continuation, a functional equation, an Euler product, and the Ramanujan
bound `a n = O(nᵉ)`.  A famous heuristic (the one quoted in the research prompt) asserts
that `S` is **countable** because "each L-function is determined by a finite set of data:
degree, conductor, root number, and Euler factors at finitely many primes."

Here we take that heuristic at face value and prove exactly what it *does* give:

* Any bookkeeping of L-functions by **genuinely finite** invariants (a `SelbergDatum`:
  degree, conductor, an integer encoding the root number, and a *finite list* of Euler
  factors) forms a countable type — `Countable SelbergDatum`.
* The same holds for L-functions parametrized by any finite algebraic datum, modeled as
  `ArithmeticLData := ℕ × ℕ × List ℤ` — `Countable ArithmeticLData`.
* A genuine, faithful sub-census: the family of **all Dirichlet characters over all
  moduli** — hence of all Dirichlet L-functions — is countable
  (`countable_dirichlet_family`).

The companion file `Uncountability.lean` supplies the contrarian counterpoint: the finite
data of "Euler factors at finitely many primes" does **not** determine an Euler product, and
the space of all admissible Euler products is uncountable.  Thus the quoted heuristic, on
its own, cannot establish countability of `S`; genuine finiteness of the parametrizing data
is exactly what is needed, and that is what these theorems isolate.

Everything here is unconditional and `sorry`-free.
-/

import Mathlib

namespace LFunctionCensus

/-- The finite invariants attached to a conjectural Selberg-class L-function, following the
heuristic "an L-function is determined by its degree, conductor, root number, and Euler
factors at finitely many primes".

* `degree`      — the degree of the functional equation;
* `conductor`   — the conductor (a positive integer, here allowed to be any `ℕ`);
* `rootNumberOrder` — an integer encoding the root number `ε` (e.g. the order of a root of
  unity, or an index into a fixed countable set of admissible values);
* `eulerFactors` — a **finite list** of local Euler factors, each recorded as its list of
  integer coefficients.

The point is that all four slots are drawn from countable data, so the aggregate is
countable. -/
structure SelbergDatum where
  degree : ℕ
  conductor : ℕ
  rootNumberOrder : ℕ
  eulerFactors : List (List ℤ)
deriving DecidableEq

/-- **The finite-invariant heuristic is countable.**  There are only countably many possible
tuples `(degree, conductor, root number, finitely many Euler factors)`.  This is the precise
content of the quoted census heuristic: if an L-function really were pinned down by such a
finite record, the resulting universe would be countable. -/
instance instCountableSelbergDatum : Countable SelbergDatum := by
  let e : SelbergDatum → ℕ × ℕ × ℕ × List (List ℤ) :=
    fun d => (d.degree, d.conductor, d.rootNumberOrder, d.eulerFactors)
  have hinj : Function.Injective e := by
    intro a b h
    cases a; cases b
    simp only [e, Prod.mk.injEq] at h
    obtain ⟨h1, h2, h3, h4⟩ := h
    subst h1; subst h2; subst h3; subst h4; rfl
  exact hinj.countable

/-- L-functions arising from a genuinely finite algebraic datum, modeled abstractly as a
triple `(degree, conductor, defining integer data)`.  The last slot `List ℤ` stands for the
finite algebraic input from which an arithmetic L-function is built (the coefficients of a
defining polynomial, a modular form's finite Hecke data, etc.). -/
abbrev ArithmeticLData : Type := ℕ × ℕ × List ℤ

/-- **Arithmetic L-functions from finite data are countable.**  Whenever an L-function is
literally produced from a finite package of integers, the family is no larger than `ℕ`. -/
theorem countable_arithmeticLData : Countable ArithmeticLData := inferInstance

/-- **A faithful sub-census: Dirichlet L-functions are countable.**  Collecting every
Dirichlet character `χ` of every modulus `N` (each individual `DirichletCharacter ℂ N` is
finite) yields a countable family — hence there are only countably many Dirichlet
L-functions.  This is an honest instance of the census: a bona-fide, uncountably-suspected-
but-actually-countable slice of the L-function universe. -/
theorem countable_dirichlet_family : Countable (Σ N : ℕ, DirichletCharacter ℂ N) :=
  inferInstance

/-- The Riemann zeta function sits at conductor `1`, degree `1`, trivial root number, with no
exceptional Euler factors: a concrete first entry of the census. -/
def riemannZetaDatum : SelbergDatum :=
  { degree := 1, conductor := 1, rootNumberOrder := 1, eulerFactors := [] }

/-- Nontriviality check: the census type has at least two distinct entries, so the
countability statements above are not vacuous.  (The zeta datum differs from the degree-`2`,
conductor-`11` datum standing in for the modular elliptic curve `11a`.) -/
theorem selbergDatum_nontrivial :
    riemannZetaDatum ≠
      { degree := 2, conductor := 11, rootNumberOrder := 1, eulerFactors := [] } := by
  decide

end LFunctionCensus

/-
# The L-Function Universe — A Cosmic Census, Part II: The Contrarian Counterpoint

The research prompt conjectures that the Selberg class is **countable** *because* "each
L-function is determined by a finite set of data (degree, conductor, root number, Euler
factors **at finitely many primes**)."  Running in contrarian mode, we test — and **refute**
— the *reasoning*, not the (widely believed) conclusion.

## The gap in the heuristic

An Euler product
`L(s) = ∏_p L_p(s)`
is, by definition, specified by a local factor `L_p` at **every** prime `p`.  Knowing the
local factors at only *finitely many* primes leaves the rest completely free.  So the space
of formal Euler products is a *function space over the primes*, and function spaces over an
infinite index set are **uncountable** as soon as there are at least two admissible local
factors at each prime (a mild condition compatible with the Ramanujan bound).

We formalize this with a two-element model of "admissible local factor at `p`" (`Bool`):

* `uncountable_euler_products` : the space `Nat.Primes → Bool` of formal Euler products is
  uncountable.
* `euler_products_not_determined_by_finite_primes` : for **any** reference product `f₀` and
  **any** finite set `S` of primes, uncountably many Euler products agree with `f₀` on all of
  `S`.  Thus the Euler factors at finitely many primes never determine the L-function — the
  precise failure of the quoted heuristic.
* `uncountable_admissible_arithmetic_functions` : made concrete, the set of `{0,1}`-valued
  arithmetic functions supported on the primes (the multiplicative seeds of such Euler
  products) is an uncountable set of honest functions `ℕ → ℤ`.

## Interpretation

None of this contradicts the belief that the *true* Selberg class is countable — that would
follow from Selberg's conjectures identifying its members with automorphic L-functions.  What
it shows is that countability is a **rigidity** phenomenon (finiteness of the underlying
arithmetic data, as isolated in `Countability.lean`), and cannot be extracted from the
"finitely many Euler factors" slogan, which by itself describes an uncountable universe.

Everything here is unconditional and `sorry`-free.
-/

import Mathlib

open Cardinal

namespace LFunctionCensus

/-- For any countably-infinite index type `α`, the space of `Bool`-valued functions on `α`
is uncountable: its cardinality is `2 ^ ℵ₀ > ℵ₀` by Cantor's theorem.  This is the abstract
engine behind the uncountability of Euler-product spaces. -/
theorem uncountable_arrow_bool {α : Type*} [Countable α] [Infinite α] :
    Uncountable (α → Bool) := by
  rw [← Cardinal.aleph0_lt_mk_iff]
  have hmk : Cardinal.mk (α → Bool) = 2 ^ ℵ₀ := by
    rw [Cardinal.mk_arrow]; simp [Cardinal.mk_eq_aleph0]
  rw [hmk]; exact Cardinal.cantor _

/-- **The space of formal Euler products is uncountable.**  Modeling "one of two admissible
local factors at each prime" by `Bool`, an Euler product is a function `Nat.Primes → Bool`.
Since there are infinitely many primes, Cantor's theorem makes this space uncountable — even
before imposing the functional equation.  Contrast this with the *countable* finite-invariant
bookkeeping of `SelbergDatum` in `Countability.lean`. -/
theorem uncountable_euler_products : Uncountable (Nat.Primes → Bool) :=
  uncountable_arrow_bool

/-- **Euler factors at finitely many primes do not determine the L-function.**

Given any reference Euler product `f₀` and any finite set `S` of primes, the collection of
Euler products agreeing with `f₀` at every prime of `S` is *still uncountable*.  In other
words, no matter how much local data one records at finitely many primes, uncountably many
distinct global Euler products remain consistent with it.

This is the sharp refutation of the prompt's reasoning "determined by ... Euler factors at
finitely many primes": that data determines nothing beyond `S`. -/
theorem euler_products_not_determined_by_finite_primes
    (f0 : Nat.Primes → Bool) (S : Finset Nat.Primes) :
    Uncountable {f : Nat.Primes → Bool // ∀ p ∈ S, f p = f0 p} := by
  classical
  have hfin : (↑S : Set Nat.Primes).Finite := S.finite_toSet
  -- the complement of a finite set of primes is still an infinite index set
  have hinf : Infinite ↥((↑S : Set Nat.Primes)ᶜ) :=
    Set.infinite_coe_iff.mpr hfin.infinite_compl
  have hU : Uncountable (↥((↑S : Set Nat.Primes)ᶜ) → Bool) :=
    uncountable_arrow_bool
  -- extend a free choice on the complement by `f0` on `S`; this is injective
  refine Function.Injective.uncountable
    (f := fun g : ↥((↑S : Set Nat.Primes)ᶜ) → Bool =>
      (⟨fun p => if h : p ∈ S then f0 p else g ⟨p, by
          rw [Set.mem_compl_iff, Finset.mem_coe]; exact h⟩, by
        intro p hp; simp [hp]⟩ :
        {f : Nat.Primes → Bool // ∀ p ∈ S, f p = f0 p})) ?_
  intro g1 g2 h
  funext q
  have hq : (q : Nat.Primes) ∉ S := by
    have hmem := q.2; rwa [Set.mem_compl_iff, Finset.mem_coe] at hmem
  have hval := congrFun (congrArg Subtype.val h) (q : Nat.Primes)
  simpa [hq] using hval

/-- **The concrete face of the phenomenon.**  The set of `{0,1}`-valued arithmetic functions
`a : ℕ → ℤ` that are supported on the primes is uncountable.  These are precisely the
functions recording, prime by prime, a binary choice of admissible local behaviour — the
multiplicative seeds of the Euler products above — and they are honest elements of the
function space `ℕ → ℤ`.  Hence the uncountability is not an artefact of an abstract index
type: it lives among genuine arithmetic functions. -/
theorem uncountable_admissible_arithmetic_functions :
    Uncountable {a : ℕ → ℤ // (∀ n, a n = 0 ∨ a n = 1) ∧ (∀ n, ¬ n.Prime → a n = 0)} := by
  classical
  haveI : Uncountable (Nat.Primes → Bool) := uncountable_euler_products
  refine Function.Injective.uncountable
    (f := fun f : Nat.Primes → Bool =>
      (⟨fun n => if h : n.Prime then (if f ⟨n, h⟩ then 1 else 0) else 0, by
        refine ⟨fun n => ?_, fun n hn => ?_⟩
        · by_cases h : n.Prime
          · simp only [h, dif_pos]; by_cases hf : f ⟨n, h⟩ <;> simp [hf]
          · simp [h]
        · simp [hn]⟩ :
        {a : ℕ → ℤ // (∀ n, a n = 0 ∨ a n = 1) ∧ (∀ n, ¬ n.Prime → a n = 0)})) ?_
  intro f g h
  funext p
  have hp : (p : ℕ).Prime := p.2
  have hval := congrFun (congrArg Subtype.val h) (p : ℕ)
  simp only [hp, dif_pos] at hval
  have hpe : (⟨(p : ℕ), hp⟩ : Nat.Primes) = p := Subtype.ext rfl
  rw [hpe] at hval
  by_cases hf : f p <;> by_cases hg : g p <;> simp [hf, hg] at hval ⊢

/-- **Synthesis (contrarian conclusion).**  Packaging the two facts: the space of formal
Euler products is uncountable, yet fixing the local data on any finite set of primes still
leaves uncountably many possibilities.  Therefore the slogan "determined by finitely many
Euler factors" is false, and cannot by itself prove the Selberg class countable. -/
theorem finite_prime_data_insufficient :

# Computational Evidence — The L-Function Census

Goal: test the prompt's conjecture that the Selberg class is countable *because* each
L-function is "determined by finite data (degree, conductor, root number, Euler factors at
finitely many primes)". Running in contrarian mode, we probe whether that *reasoning* holds.

## 1. Small cases: the census by conductor

Ordering known L-functions by conductor (arithmetic normalization), the beginning of the
census is genuinely countable and well populated:

| conductor | degree | example L-function            |
|-----------|--------|-------------------------------|
| 1         | 1      | Riemann zeta ζ(s)             |
| 1         | 2      | L(s, Δ) (weight-12 cusp form) |
| 3,4,5,... | 1      | Dirichlet L(s, χ) (χ mod N)   |
| 11        | 2      | L(s, E), E = elliptic curve 11a|
| 15,17,... | 2      | modular forms / elliptic curves|

Each conductor supports only finitely many entries of bounded degree, and there are
countably many conductors — consistent with countability of the *arithmetic* families.

## 2. Counting the concrete families

* Dirichlet characters: for each modulus `N`, `DirichletCharacter ℂ N` is a **finite** group
  (of size `φ(N)`), and there are countably many `N`. Union = countable.
  Formalized: `LFunctionCensus.countable_dirichlet_family`.
* Elliptic curves over ℚ: parametrized by pairs `(a, b) ∈ ℚ²` (short Weierstrass) → countable.
* Finite-invariant records `(degree, conductor, root number, finite Euler list)` → countable.
  Formalized: `LFunctionCensus.instCountableSelbergDatum`.

## 3. Counterexample hunt — the flaw in the heuristic

The heuristic claims "Euler factors at **finitely many** primes" determine the L-function.
Test: an Euler product `∏_p L_p(s)` is a *function on the set of all primes*. If at each
prime there are ≥ 2 admissible local factors (true under Ramanujan; e.g. two allowed Satake
pairs), then:

* fixing the local factors on any finite set `S` of primes leaves the factors at the
  infinitely many primes outside `S` completely free;
* the number of completions is `2^(#{primes} - #S) = 2^ℵ₀`, which is **uncountable**.

Concrete diagonal witness (Cantor): enumerate primes `p₀ < p₁ < p₂ < …`; for any proposed
countable list of Euler products `f₀, f₁, f₂, …`, the product taking the *opposite* choice of
`fₖ` at `pₖ` differs from every `fₖ`, so no countable list exhausts them.

**Result of the hunt:** the heuristic's reasoning fails — the "finitely many primes" data is
not determining. This is a genuine disproof (of the *argument*), formalized as
`LFunctionCensus.euler_products_not_determined_by_finite_primes` and
`LFunctionCensus.uncountable_euler_products`, with a concrete arithmetic-function version
`LFunctionCensus.uncountable_admissible_arithmetic_functions`.

## 4. Reconciliation

Countability of the *true* Selberg class (widely believed) is a **rigidity** statement: it
needs the members to come from genuinely finite arithmetic data (automorphy / Selberg's
conjectures), not merely to have Euler products. The positive theorems isolate exactly the
countable-from-finite-data content; the negative theorems show the "finitely many Euler
factors" slogan is by itself insufficient.

## 5. Sequences / OEIS

The count of primitive Dirichlet characters by modulus follows `φ`-type data; the running
tally of arithmetic L-functions by conductor is not a single clean OEIS entry (it mixes
degrees and sources), so no specific OEIS ID is claimed here.

concept.concept_description: Euclid's parallel postulate says parallel lines never meet. Hyperbolic geometry says they can diverge. Elliptic geometry says they converge. But what about a geometry where parallel lines BOTH converge AND diverge? Define a Split Geometry on R^2 where the parallel postulate is direction-dependent: lines parallel to the x-axis diverge (hyperbolic behavior) while lines parallel to the y-axis converge (elliptic behavior). The metric is ds^2 = dx^2/cosh^2(y) + dy^2 * cosh^2(x) — expanding in x and contracting in y. Conjecture: Split Geometry is a consistent Riemannian geometry with curvature K(x,y) = -sech^2(y) + sech^2(x) that changes sign across the diagonals. The geometry has a 'phase boundary' along the lines y = x and y = -x where K = 0 (flat). In the region |x| > |y|, K > 0 (elliptic) and in the region |y| > |x|, K < 0 (hyperbolic). The geodesics in split geometry are piecewise combinations of exponential curves (in hyperbolic regions) and trigonometric curves (in elliptic regions). Test: compute the Christoffel symbols and curvature tensor for the split metric. Prove that geodesics cross the phase boundary at most twice. Compute the area of a split triangle with one vertex in each region. Impact: a geometry where the curvature of space depends on which direction you look — the mathematical realization of a universe that is simultaneously expanding and contracting.

  · exact Or.inr (Or.inl ⟨(K_eq_zero_iff_abs x y).mpr h, h⟩)
  · exact Or.inr (Or.inr ⟨K_neg_of_abs_lt x y h, h⟩)

/-! ### Crossing the phase boundary at most twice -/

/-- **Geodesic/line crossing bound (algebraic core).** Consider a straight
coordinate line `t ↦ (x₀ + t·a, y₀ + t·b)` that is *not* parallel to either
diagonal, i.e. `a² ≠ b²`.  Then among any three parameters `t₁, t₂, t₃` at which
the point lies on the phase boundary `{x² = y²}`, two must coincide.  In other
words, the line meets the phase boundary in at most two distinct points. -/
theorem geodesic_crosses_at_most_twice (a b x0 y0 t1 t2 t3 : ℝ) (hab : a ^ 2 ≠ b ^ 2)
    (h1 : (x0 + t1 * a) ^ 2 = (y0 + t1 * b) ^ 2)
    (h2 : (x0 + t2 * a) ^ 2 = (y0 + t2 * b) ^ 2)
    (h3 : (x0 + t3 * a) ^ 2 = (y0 + t3 * b) ^ 2) :
    t1 = t2 ∨ t1 = t3 ∨ t2 = t3 := by
  by_contra h
  push_neg at h
  obtain ⟨h12, h13, h23⟩ := h
  have e12 : (t1 - t2) * ((a ^ 2 - b ^ 2) * (t1 + t2) + 2 * (x0 * a - y0 * b)) = 0 := by
    nlinarith [h1, h2]
  have e13 : (t1 - t3) * ((a ^ 2 - b ^ 2) * (t1 + t3) + 2 * (x0 * a - y0 * b)) = 0 := by
    nlinarith [h1, h3]
  have f12 : (a ^ 2 - b ^ 2) * (t1 + t2) + 2 * (x0 * a - y0 * b) = 0 := by
    rcases mul_eq_zero.1 e12 with h | h
    · exact absurd (by linarith : t1 = t2) h12
    · exact h
  have f13 : (a ^ 2 - b ^ 2) * (t1 + t3) + 2 * (x0 * a - y0 * b) = 0 := by
    rcases mul_eq_zero.1 e13 with h | h
    · exact absurd (by linarith : t1 = t3) h13
    · exact h
  have hz : (a ^ 2 - b ^ 2) * (t2 - t3) = 0 := by nlinarith [f12, f13]
  rcases mul_eq_zero.1 hz with h | h
  · exact hab (by linarith)
  · exact h23 (by linarith)

/-- **Geodesic/line crossing bound (stated via `K`).** A straight coordinate
line not parallel to a diagonal (`a² ≠ b²`) crosses the phase boundary `K = 0`
at most twice: among any three parameters at which `K` vanishes along the line,
two coincide. -/
theorem line_crosses_phaseBoundary_at_most_twice
    (a b x0 y0 t1 t2 t3 : ℝ) (hab : a ^ 2 ≠ b ^ 2)
    (h1 : K (x0 + t1 * a) (y0 + t1 * b) = 0)
    (h2 : K (x0 + t2 * a) (y0 + t2 * b) = 0)
    (h3 : K (x0 + t3 * a) (y0 + t3 * b) = 0) :
    t1 = t2 ∨ t1 = t3 ∨ t2 = t3 :=
  geodesic_crosses_at_most_twice a b x0 y0 t1 t2 t3 hab
    ((K_eq_zero_iff_sq _ _).mp h1)
    ((K_eq_zero_iff_sq _ _).mp h2)
    ((K_eq_zero_iff_sq _ _).mp h3)

end SplitGeometry

/-
# Surreal Topology: A Bridge Between Combinatorial Game Theory and Point-Set Topology

Conway's surreal numbers `Surreal` form the largest totally ordered field, built out of
combinatorial games (`PGame`).  A natural topology to put on them is the **order topology**
(a.k.a. the *interval topology*), generated by the open rays `Set.Iio a` and `Set.Ioi a`,
equivalently by the open intervals `(a, b)`.

This file proves a cross-domain **connector theorem**:

> The order/interval topology on the surreal numbers is **disconnected**.

The bridge is between:

* *Combinatorial game theory / order theory*: the surreals are **non-Archimedean** — there is a
  single surreal number larger than every natural number.  This is a genuinely game-theoretic
  fact here, obtained from `Surreal.bddAbove_range_of_small`: any *set-sized* family of surreals
  is bounded above, and `ℕ` is set-sized, so `{0, 1, 2, …}` has a surreal upper bound.

* *Point-set topology*: that single non-Archimedean gap splits the line into two nonempty pieces
  that are simultaneously open and closed (a nontrivial *clopen* set), so the space cannot be
  (pre)connected.

The clopen set exhibited is the collection of **finite surreals**
`{x | ∃ n : ℕ, x < n}` — everything dominated by some natural number.  Its complement is the class
of infinitely large surreals.  Both are open in the order topology, so the finite surreals form a
nontrivial clopen set.

## Consequences (refuting the naive "connected / contractible" conjecture)

Because a path-connected (in particular, contractible) space is connected, the disconnectedness
result immediately shows the interval topology on `Surreal` is **not** connected, **not**
path-connected, and hence **not** contractible.  So the conjecture that the interval topology makes
`No` a connected, contractible space is *false*; the honest statement is the opposite.

## Main results

* `Surreal.exists_gt_natCast` : non-Archimedean witness — a surreal above every natural number.
* `Surreal.finiteSurreals_isClopen` : the finite surreals form a clopen set.
* `Surreal.not_preconnectedSpace` : the interval topology on `Surreal` is disconnected.
* `Surreal.not_connectedSpace`, `Surreal.not_pathConnectedSpace` : corollaries.
* `Surreal.instT2Space` : as a positive counterpoint, the interval topology *is* Hausdorff.
-/

import Mathlib

open Set

namespace Surreal

/-!
### The interval (order) topology on the surreal numbers

We equip `Surreal.{0}` with the order topology.  Since `Preorder.topology` is *defined* as the
topology generated by the open rays, the `OrderTopology` instance holds by `rfl`.
-/

noncomputable instance instTopologicalSpace : TopologicalSpace Surreal.{0} :=
  Preorder.topology Surreal.{0}

instance instOrderTopology : OrderTopology Surreal.{0} := ⟨rfl⟩

/-- Positive counterpoint: the interval topology on the surreals is Hausdorff, being the
order topology on a linear order. -/
instance instT2Space : T2Space Surreal.{0} := inferInstance

/-!
### The game-theoretic ingredient: the surreals are non-Archimedean

`Surreal.bddAbove_range_of_small` says any family of surreals indexed by a *set* (a `Small` type)
is bounded above.  Applying this to the natural numbers produces a surreal dominating every
natural number — a purely order/game-theoretic fact with no topological content.
-/

/-- **Non-Archimedean witness.**  There is a surreal number strictly greater than every natural
number.  (The surreal upper bound of the set `{0, 1, 2, …}` exists because that set is small.) -/
theorem exists_gt_natCast : ∃ M : Surreal.{0}, ∀ n : ℕ, (n : Surreal.{0}) < M := by
  obtain ⟨M, hM⟩ := Surreal.bddAbove_range_of_small (fun n : ℕ => (n : Surreal.{0}))
  refine ⟨M + 1, fun n => ?_⟩
  have hle : (n : Surreal.{0}) ≤ M := hM ⟨n, rfl⟩
  have h1 : M < M + 1 := by linarith [zero_lt_one (α := Surreal.{0})]
  linarith

/-!
### The clopen set of finite surreals
-/

/-- The **finite surreals**: those bounded above by some natural number. -/
def FiniteSurreals : Set Surreal.{0} := {x | ∃ n : ℕ, x < (n : Surreal.{0})}

/-- The finite surreals are open: they are the union of the open rays `Iio n`. -/
theorem finiteSurreals_isOpen : IsOpen FiniteSurreals := by
  have hrw : FiniteSurreals = ⋃ n : ℕ, Iio (n : Surreal.{0}) := by
    ext x; simp [FiniteSurreals]
  rw [hrw]
  exact isOpen_iUnion (fun _ => isOpen_Iio)

/-- The finite surreals are closed: their complement (the infinitely large surreals) is open,
since around any infinite surreal `x` the whole ray `Ioi (x - 1)` stays infinite. -/
theorem finiteSurreals_isClosed : IsClosed FiniteSurreals := by
  rw [← isOpen_compl_iff, isOpen_iff_forall_mem_open]
  intro x hx
  simp only [FiniteSurreals, mem_compl_iff, mem_setOf_eq, not_exists, not_lt] at hx
  refine ⟨Ioi (x - 1), ?_, isOpen_Ioi, by simp⟩
  intro y hy
  simp only [mem_Ioi] at hy
  simp only [FiniteSurreals, mem_compl_iff, mem_setOf_eq, not_exists, not_lt]
  intro n
  have hn : ((n : ℕ) : Surreal.{0}) + 1 ≤ x := by
    have := hx (n + 1)
    push_cast at this ⊢
    linarith
  linarith

/-- The finite surreals form a nontrivial **clopen** set. -/
theorem finiteSurreals_isClopen : IsClopen FiniteSurreals :=
  ⟨finiteSurreals_isClosed, finiteSurreals_isOpen⟩

/-- `0` is a finite surreal, so the clopen set is nonempty. -/
theorem zero_mem_finiteSurreals : (0 : Surreal.{0}) ∈ FiniteSurreals :=
  ⟨1, by norm_num⟩

/-- Some surreal is *not* finite (any non-Archimedean witness), so the clopen set is not
everything. -/
theorem finiteSurreals_ne_univ : FiniteSurreals ≠ (univ : Set Surreal.{0}) := by
  obtain ⟨M, hM⟩ := exists_gt_natCast
  intro h
  have hMmem : M ∈ FiniteSurreals := by rw [h]; trivial
  obtain ⟨n, hn⟩ := hMmem
  exact absurd hn (not_lt.2 (le_of_lt (hM n)))

/-!
### The connector theorem and its topological corollaries
-/

/-- **Main connector theorem.**  The interval (order) topology on the surreal numbers is
disconnected: the finite surreals form a nontrivial clopen set.  This bridges the
game-theoretic non-Archimedean structure of `Surreal` with a point-set topological property,
and refutes the conjecture that the interval topology is connected. -/
theorem not_preconnectedSpace : ¬ PreconnectedSpace Surreal.{0} := by
  intro h
  rcases isClopen_iff.1 finiteSurreals_isClopen with h0 | h1
  · exact (h0 ▸ zero_mem_finiteSurreals : (0 : Surreal.{0}) ∈ (∅ : Set Surreal.{0}))
  · exact finiteSurreals_ne_univ h1

/-- The surreal line with the interval topology is not connected. -/
theorem not_connectedSpace : ¬ ConnectedSpace Surreal.{0} := by
  intro h
  exact not_preconnectedSpace h.toPreconnectedSpace

/-- The surreal line with the interval topology is not path-connected (hence not contractible):
a path-connected space is connected, but the surreals are disconnected. -/
theorem not_pathConnectedSpace : ¬ PathConnectedSpace Surreal.{0} := by
  intro h
  exact not_connectedSpace h.connectedSpace

end Surreal
